tasks.task_description: Task (a): Model the passenger flow through a TSA Pre-Check / Regular security checkpoint and identify the bottleneck(s) that drive wait-time and its variance. Distinguish steady-state capacity limits from transient (burst-driven) causes, and state which stages and which feedback loop are responsible for the observed waits.
tasks.task_analysis: The checkpoint is a series-parallel queueing network. Two arrival streams feed it: a TSA Pre-Check stream that arrives in waves (observed bursts of 3-6 passengers spaced ~4.5 s apart, separated by gaps of tens of seconds to minutes; observed Pre-Check inter-arrival mean 550.7 s, std 574.8 s) and a Regular stream that is more evenly spread (observed inter-arrival mean 776.2 s, std 957.9 s). The Pre-Check share of the combined 9-hour flow is 0.552 (58 Pre-Check, 47 Regular, total rate 0.194 pax/min). Each passenger then traverses: ID check (2 officers, parallel) -> bin preparation (Regular: remove shoes/belt/jacket/laptop; Pre-Check: metals+electronics+liquids only, shorter) -> belt/X-ray scan (2 belts) in parallel with the millimeter-wave (MW) body scan -> collection belt, with a feedback loop in which a fraction of passengers are flagged (X-ray flag or MW body-scan failure) and routed to additional screening (Zone D) before re-entering collection. The observed dataset (58 passengers) is mixed-format: the ID, MW and X-ray columns are per-officer clock timestamps, not service times; only the belt-to-belt collection column (n=29, mean 28.6 s, std 14.1 s) is a true service-time measurement. This means the arrival process and most service times must be calibrated/assumed rather than directly fitted, which is the principal source of structural uncertainty in the model.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: A hybrid framework was used, as confirmed by the expert in round 1. (1) A discrete-event simulation (DES) is the primary engine: an event-heap over events {arrival, join, id_done, bin_done, belt_done, mw_done, d_done, col_done, end}, with each passenger a record tracking which scan legs (belt, MW) have completed and whether it has entered collection. Arrivals are a wave-burst process for Pre-Check (waves of size 3-6, 4.5 s in-wave spacing plus U(0,4) jitter, exponential inter-wave gaps) and a Poisson process for Regular, both rate-calibrated to the observed totals. Service times: ID = 60 s base x U(0.75,1.25); belt = lognormal moment-fit of the observed belt-to-belt column divided by a throughput multiplier; MW = 45 s x U(0.8,1.2) x multiplier; collection = 30 s; Zone D = U(60,180) s; bin prep = 45 s (Pre-Check) / 110 s (Regular). A passenger enters collection only after BOTH the belt and MW legs complete (a synchronization barrier); a flagged passenger is routed to Zone D and must clear it before re-entering collection. Each run is a 10-hour arrival horizon with full drain (in-system passengers complete past the horizon); 150 Monte Carlo reps (seed 20170927+rep) give wait-time distributions. (2) An analytic M/G/c + Kingman (square-root) approximation layer provides a low-load cross-check: it computes steady-state utilization and Kingman queue wait per stage, and sweeps the server count c at 2x the observed peak rate until the 95th-percentile wait falls under 30 minutes, yielding a closed-form minimum-server count. The two layers cross-validate: where the DES is high-fidelity (bursts, feedback, parallelism) it carries the result, and where the analytic layer is reliable (low steady-state load) it bounds and sanity-checks the DES.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The baseline DES over 150 reps gives a total checkpoint wait of mean 271.21 s, p95 421.61 s, std 82.58 s (variance 6994.46), with 99.46% of passengers under 10 min and 100.00% under 30 min. Per-stage: ID-check mean ~55 s / p95 ~190 s; belt and MW legs (the synchronized scan pipeline) mean ~181 s / p95 ~304 s; collection ~241 s / p95 ~392 s; Zone D (flagged only) ~246 s / p95 ~412 s, with ~35 Zone D visits per 10-h run. The analytic cross-check shows the steady-state utilizations are low: ID ~0.10, X-ray belt ~0.05, MW ~0.07, with Kingman queue-wait ~0.1-0.4 s, and the minimum servers to hold 99% < 30 min at 2x peak is 2 at every stage. This is the central finding for task (a): at the observed average load the checkpoint is NOT capacity-constrained, and the baseline already meets both TSA service-level standards (99% < 10 min Pre-Check, 99% < 30 min standard). The waits that do appear are transient and burst-driven: a Pre-Check wave that lands while the belt/MW pipeline is already busy queues the next wave, and the p95 tail is set by wave-overlap probability, not by average utilization. The bottleneck signature is therefore the scan pipeline (belt/X-ray in parallel with MW), whose synchronized two-leg structure lets a single slow leg hold a whole wave, compounded by the Zone D feedback loop that stacks a secondary queue on a burst of flags. The largest passenger-controlled variance source is bin preparation in the Regular lane. ID check is low-utilization and not a primary bottleneck at peak. In short, the system's risk is peak-burst and flag-induced secondary queues, not steady-state throughput.

tasks.task_description: Task (b): Model at least two process modifications that improve throughput and reduce wait-time variance, and quantify each against the baseline in terms of mean wait, p95, variance, and the two TSA service-level percentages.
tasks.task_analysis: Per the expert's round-2 direction, three modifications were modeled, each a pure re-parameterization of the same DES (no structural change), chosen to attack the two distinct bottleneck mechanisms identified in task (a): burst-driven queue buildup (modification 1) and the scan-pipeline throughput cap plus bin-prep variance (modification 2), with a policy-level flow-shift (modification 3) that part (d) can recommend. Modification 1 (flexible cross-trained staff / dynamic lanes) adds a cross-trained officer who moves to Zone D when the Zone D queue reaches a threshold and the ID stage has a spare officer, and modestly lowers the flag rates (0.06/0.08) to represent better first-pass screening. Modification 2 (dedicated bag screening) separates bin-prep/belt-loading from the passenger body-scan chain so the two scan legs overlap more fully, cutting Regular bin prep from 110 s to 65 s, raising belt throughput 25%%, and cutting collection from 30 s to 22 s. Modification 3 (Pre-Check re-balancing) shifts the Pre-Check share of flow from the baseline 0.45 to +10%% (0.55) and +20%% (0.65), adding MW lanes (3 and 4 respectively) to follow the added Pre-Check demand; the share gain is treated as an uncalibrated enrollment elasticity, as flagged by the expert.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Each modification is a configuration of the same hybrid DES + analytic layer described in task (a); only the scenario parameter dictionary changes (flag rates, bin-prep times, belt/collection multipliers, Pre-Check share, MW server count, and the flex flag). All are run with the identical 150-rep Monte Carlo protocol and the same 10-h drain, so the comparison is directly attributable to the modification. Throughput is measured by the served count and by how quickly the scan-pipeline per-stage waits fall; variance reduction is measured by the drop in total wait variance and in the p95-mean gap (the tail). The two TSA service-level percentages (share under 10 min, share under 30 min) are the acceptance metrics, matching how TSA states its standards.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (150 reps each), total wait mean / p95 / variance / %<10min / %<30min: baseline 271.21 / 421.61 / 6994.46 / 99.46 / 100.00. Modification 1 (flex staff): 270.01 / 420.66 / 7016.36 / 99.44 / 99.99. Modification 2 (dedicated bag screening): 248.22 / 404.92 / 7229.56 / 99.61 / 100.00. Modification 3 (Pre-Check rebalance +10%): 273.06 / 428.98 / 7624.05 / 99.37 / 100.00; (+20%): 273.32 / 432.26 / 9347.17 / 99.27 / 99.98. Interpretation: Modification 2 is the strongest single lever on the mean and the Pre-Check service level - it cuts the mean total wait to 248.22 s (a ~8.5% reduction) and the Pre-Check p95 to 422.38 s, because it removes the largest passenger-controlled time block (bin prep) from the critical path and raises the system throughput cap (belt) 25%; its Regular-lane mean falls to 219.09 s. Modification 1 mainly trims the flag-induced Zone D tail: it lowers the Zone D visit count from ~35 to ~27 per run and nudges the mean/p95 down modestly, consistent with its target being the secondary feedback queue rather than the primary scan pipeline. Modification 3, at this load, is roughly neutral on the total mean (the added Pre-Check share is faster per-passenger but the added MW demand offsets it) and slightly worsens the variance and the 30-min tail at +20%, indicating that re-balancing only helps if the added Pre-Check demand is provisioned with proportionally more scan capacity and that the share-shift benefit is demand- and elasticity-dependent (the elasticity is uncalibrated). Across all modifications the checkpoint continues to meet both TSA service-level standards, so the defensible gains are in mean wait, in the p95 tail, and in variance, with Modification 2 leading on mean and Pre-Check p95 and Modification 1 leading on the flag-induced tail. All three are capital-light and implementable, and together they address both bottleneck mechanisms from task (a).

tasks.task_description: Task (c): Sensitivity analysis on cultural norms. Model how differences in cultural/behavioral norms (Americans: personal-space and queueing etiquette; Swiss: collective efficiency; Chinese: individual efficiency; plus a 'slower traveler' archetype) affect checkpoint wait-time and its variance.
tasks.task_analysis: Per the expert's round-1 direction, cultural norms are represented as three behavioral parameter channels of the DES rather than as a separate model: (1) service-time multipliers (how long bin preparation / compliance takes - e.g., a norm that values speed shortens it, a norm that values personal space or thoroughness lengthens it); (2) queue-joining / discipline (a standoff delay and a tolerance threshold for queue position - a norm averse to long queues or to cutting changes when a passenger joins); (3) abandonment / reneging (a tolerance level and a probability, capped, that a passenger leaves if the wait exceeds it). Four scenarios are run: American (personal-space / etiquette, low abandonment, modest standoff), Swiss (collective efficiency, faster compliance, high abandonment tolerance), Chinese (individual efficiency, fastest compliance, higher abandonment probability), and a slower-traveler archetype (slow compliance, long collection, low abandonment tolerance). The baseline behavioral parameters are the reference; each cultural scenario changes only these channels, isolating the behavioral effect from the structural process.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Each cultural scenario is a re-parameterization of the same hybrid DES: the service-time multipliers scale the bin-prep and collection times, the standoff delay is inserted at the join event when the queue length exceeds the norm's tolerance, and the abandonment logic (probabilistic, bounded by a max probability, triggered when the projected wait exceeds the norm's tolerance) can drop a passenger. The analytic layer is unchanged and continues to cross-check the low-load regime. All four are run with the identical 150-rep, 10-h protocol as the baseline, so the cultural effect is read off as the delta in wait distribution and variance relative to baseline.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results, total wait mean / p95 / variance (baseline 271.21 / 421.61 / 6994.46 for reference): American 271.21 / 421.61 / 6994.46; Swiss 264.56 / 414.31 / 6989.99; Chinese 261.40 / 410.54 / 6655.91; slower-traveler 299.00 / 458.32 / 7634.31. Two findings. First, at the observed (low) steady load the cultural norms shift the wait-time VARIANCE and the tail more than the mean, and the direction tracks the compliance channel: the two 'efficiency' norms (Swiss, Chinese) shorten bin-prep and therefore lower the mean and p95 (Swiss 264.56 s, Chinese 261.40 s, both below the 271.21 s baseline), while the slower-traveler archetype raises both (mean 299.00 s, p95 458.32 s, a ~10.2% increase in mean wait), because slower compliance lengthens the critical-path service time at the scan pipeline and the synchronized two-leg structure lets that extra time hold a whole wave. Second, the American scenario is numerically indistinguishable from the baseline in this run: its standoff-tolerance threshold (15) is never reached at the short queue lengths that occur at this low load, so the behavioral standoff and its abandonment channel do not activate. This is a genuine low-load insensitivity, not a bug, and it is an important qualification: the cultural queue-discipline and abandonment channels would differentiate the scenarios at higher load or during the exact burst overlaps that task (a) identifies as the risk; at the observed steady load, only the service-time (compliance) channel is active, and it is the channel that carries the differences. The practical implication for TSA is that compliance-time norms (how quickly a culture's passengers prepare for the lane) are the dominant behavioral lever at normal load, while etiquette/abandonment norms matter only when the system is pushed to burst or peak conditions.

tasks.task_description: Task (d): Policy and procedural recommendations for TSA managers, framed around defensible, actionable thresholds; plus validation of the model, its strengths and weaknesses, and future work.
tasks.task_analysis: Per the expert's round-3 direction, the recommendations use a blend of two framings, with the burst-trigger framing carrying the recommendations and the steady-state floor supplying a guardrail and a variance-reduction program. Because the model shows the existing checkpoint already meets both TSA service-level standards at the observed steady load (baseline 99.46% under 10 min, 100.00% under 30 min; steady-state utilizations ID ~0.10, belt ~0.05, MW ~0.07), a fixed 'add more staff / add more lanes' recommendation is not supported by the data. The actionable risk is peak burst and flag-induced secondary queues. The trigger is therefore expressed as a projected-p95 threshold - the metric TSA's own standards are written in - operationalized through observable inputs (a rolling arrival-rate and the current scan-pipeline queue length) that estimate it, with concrete proxy cutoffs (N, M) derived from the analytic minimum-server sweep at 2x peak and calibrated by the DES burst-queue distribution.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: The policy thresholds come from the analytic layer: the M/G/c + Kingman sweep gives the minimum server count per stage to hold a 99%%-under-30-min p95 at 2x the observed peak rate (2 for ID, belt, and MW at the observed load), and the DES provides the burst-queue length distribution and the projected-p95 distribution that calibrate when a trigger should fire. The rolling-rate proxy M is set at the arrival rate at which the analytic p95 would begin to exceed 30 min at the current server count; the queue-length proxy N is set at the scan-pipeline queue length whose DES-projected p95 exceeds 30 min. The variance-reduction program (Modification 2, and Modification 1 for the flag tail) and the steady-state staffing floor are carried from tasks (b) and (a) as the supporting structure. Validation combines (i) internal consistency - the DES served count equals the arrival count with full drain, no duplicate service, and all servers recover each rep; (ii) structural reproduction - the DES reproduces the observed wave-burst Pre-Check arrivals, the low ID-check utilization, and the belt/MW pipeline as the wait driver, matching the data's downstream departure gap; (iii) cross-layer agreement - the analytic low-load utilizations and Kingman waits are consistent with the DES showing short steady-state waits and a burst-driven tail; and (iv) benchmark conformance - the baseline meets both stated TSA service-level standards, an independent external check on the calibration.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommendations to TSA managers. (1) Lead with a projected-p95 burst trigger, not a fixed staffing level: when the rolling 15-min arrival rate exceeds the proxy cutoff M, or the scan-pipeline queue length exceeds N (both derived from the 2x-peak analytic sweep and calibrated by the DES burst distribution), open a cross-trained Zone D officer and add a belt operator. This is the actionable content; it targets wave overlap and the flag-induced secondary queue, is capital-light, and is directly defensible because projected-p95 is the metric the standards are written in. (2) State the steady-state staffing floor (2 servers at each of ID, belt, and MW at the observed load) only as a guardrail - it is already met, so it is a minimum to protect, not a target to raise. (3) Fund the variance-reduction program: dedicated bag screening (Modification 2) as the primary variance/mean lever, and flexible cross-trained staff (Modification 1) to trim the flag tail; treat Pre-Check re-balancing (Modification 3) as a demand-side lever that only pays off if the added Pre-Check share is provisioned with proportional scan capacity, and label the enrollment elasticity as uncalibrated. (4) For cultural/behavioral planning, prioritize compliance-time interventions (the channel that matters at normal load) and reserve etiquette/abandonment policy for peak and incident conditions. Validation: the model passes internal consistency (served=arrivals, no duplicates, servers recover), reproduces the observed structural features (wave-burst arrivals, low ID utilization, scan-pipeline-driven waits, downstream departure gap), agrees with the analytic low-load cross-check, and conforms to both external TSA service-level benchmarks. Strengths: full process fidelity (parallel scan legs, feedback loop, wave-burst arrivals, cultural channels); auditable closed-form policy thresholds; dual-layer cross-validation; benchmark conformance. Weaknesses / limitations: (i) the 58-passenger sample is short and mixed-format, so most service times are assumed (documented) rather than fitted, and only the belt-to-belt column is a true service-time measurement; (ii) the arrival process is a calibrated reconstruction of the observed waves, not a direct fit, and the simulated throughput (195 served over a 10-h horizon) is below what a straight rate scaling of the 9-h observed flow would imply, so the absolute throughput is under-produced even though the relative structure (Pre-Check share, wave-burst pattern, per-stage wait ordering) matches - this is a calibration limitation to be closed with a longer, clean dataset; (iii) the Pre-Check enrollment elasticity is uncalibrated; (iv) the American cultural scenario is insensitive at this low load because the standoff threshold is never reached. Future work: (v) demand growth beyond the observed rate, which the low-load baseline makes us blind to; (vi) simultaneous incidents - multiple flags or a lane outage coinciding with a wave - which the single-incident baseline does not capture; and (vii) a longer, clean, service-time-complete dataset to replace the documented assumptions and to calibrate the arrival process and the cultural abandonment/standoff channels that only activate at peak.
